PROLEGOMENA. 


ORE than ten yeara ago, when R.v. Roth sug: 
{ gested to me to supply the place of Wester- 
gaard’s edition of the Avesta, already out of 
print, by @ revised edition of the text, I undertook the 
work after some hesitation, encouraged, however, by the 
thought that a few years would suffice for the completion 
of the task. Such was my hope and expectation, but 
the mass of material which collected, and other circum- 
stances more especially, have long deferred the wished- 
for completion of the task imposed. With the Vendidad, 
however, the Avesth proper is at last concluded, and 
T hasten to finish the work, and with the present Pro- 
legomena to give the clue to the whole. 

Wi tay be allowed in the first place to say a few 
words regarding the work accomplished by my pre- 
decessor N. L. Westergaard, and the edition of the 
Zendavesta which he brought out in the year 1854, 
1 think I'am perhaps better qualified than any one else 
to pass judgment on this subject; for I have carefully 
examined anew, and have fully tested, all the means ahd 
resources which were at Westergaard’s command. 
I may say at once that he succeeded marvellously in 
accomplishing that most difficult task, an editio princepg 
of the Avestd. So admirably did Westergaard work 
through the manuscripts that were known to him, and 
so model the text he provided, that without entirely new 
manuscript material, there would have remained little or 
sothing for me to do. A rereading of the texts extent 


in Europe, I found, promised but little fruit. It soon 
‘became evident, however, that in India there was hidden 
an unopened store of manuscripts, and I forthwith directed 
my attention to securing these. Through the kindness 
of friends I succeeded in procuring the greater number of 
them, and those the more important; this circumstance has 
placed me in a position to improve upon Westergaard 
in details, or in cases where he had already hit upon the 
right reading—as for the most part he had—to substan- 
tiate this by better authority. Taken as a whole, my 
work has remaincd, what was intended from the first, an 
improved reprint of Westergaard. Only the critical 
apparatus has unfortunately greatly increased in extent 
and compass. a 
Especially for the Yasna much new material Became 
accessible to me. In the Yashts, the one ancestral manu- 
script has placed thé text criticism on a firmer basis, 
In the Vendidad, on the contrary, I have not been 
able to get much beyond Westeg#kard's material. 
Tt is particularly to he regretted that some of the Yasna 
manuscripts came to hand late; some in fact even after 
the printing was finished. All the more unfortunate was 
this, as among the stragglers were some that at the 
utset were almost indispensable, as regards text criti- 
cism, for a proper classification and estimation” of the 


manuacripts.

a sketch, alphabetically"atr d for easier survey, of all

Most of the manuscripts, irrespective of the corrections 
of the copyists themselves, are corrected by a second, 
and sometimes by a third hand. The distinction between 
manuscripts of Iranian and of Indian origin iy important. 
The Iranian manuscripts ure casily recognized by the 
characteristic features of tne script and by the uniformly 
well-marked letters with hvavy horizontal and light vertical 
strokes. The Indian writing varies considerably accurd- 
ing tu the scribe and the time. 

The classitication of the manuscripts may best be 
begun with the Vendidad, for in this the relationship ot 
the manuscripts i» simplest and clearest. The manuscripts 
with Pahlavi translation are to be taken as the basis. This 
class of manuscripts is represented by Kr-Lq. 1 have 
Mot succeeded in finding, even in transcripts, the trace 
of a third cognate ancestral manuseript of the Pahlavi

The second class is composed of the Mss. of the 
so-called Vendidad sada, in which the Yasna, Vispered 
and Vendidad are all combined, without the Pahlavi trans- 
lation, into a single book for liturgical usc.t Among the 
great mass of Vendidad sada Mas., the Persian ones are 
distinguished by differences su marked that Wester- 
gaard even set up two distinct classes, namely, the 
Indian Vendidad sadas and those from Yersia. 

The arrangement of the texts in all Mss. of the Ven- 
didad sada, including the Persian, is the same. In the 
case of repetitions, while the Pahlavi Vendidid prefers 
abbreviating or abridging, the Vendidad sada, especially 
in the Vendidad, avoids thix; the text is given by the 
latter almost always in cxtenso. In general, in the case 
of greater divergences, the text of the Vendidad sidas ty 
the fuller, that of the Pahlavi Vendidads is the more brief. 

By no means rare is the case where all the Vendidid 
sddas agree in a majority of single words of clauses as 
opposed to a minority in the Pallavi Vendiddd. In the 
case of the single Vendidad sada Mss, differences arining: 
from omissions or additions are very rare, All Mss. of 
the Vendidad sida ultimately presuppose a common arche- 
type. There seems to me to be no doubt that this arche- 
type in turn was excerpted and compiled from the Pahlavi 
Avesta Mss. We can hardly conceive of the Vendidid 
of the Sassanians without the Pahlavitranslation, As a 
direct proof of this may be instanced numerous Avesta 
glosses of the Pahlavi translation which have crept into 
the Avesta text of the Vendidad sida. In separating the 
Avesta text from its Pahlavi setting several mistakes may 
have been made by the compiler of the Vendidad sada, 
namely in cases where the text was abridged and he tried 
to give it complete. Our Pahlavi Vendidads often leave 
us in the dark as to the extent of an abridgment, for 
they forget to give the catchword after the sign of ab- 
breviation & (vad ‘‘as far as").

From the last examples especially, we can plainly sev 
that there existed also in lran a Vulgate text, generally in- 
ferior, which here and there influenced the copyists. ‘Taking 
them for all in all I should be inclined to follow the view 
of Westergaard, that in the Iranian Vendidid sAdas we 
have the descendants of a critical revision, or new redac- 
tion of the text. This revision was at first an external one. 
Certain orthographic principles which also the younger 
copyists in ran followed, were carricd out. Among 
these I count the preference for == instead of my, Aw; 
for Gey. tev instead of -few; for w at the end instead of » 
Sometimes the editor may have allowed himself to be 
influenced by the Pahlavi translation, c.g. new in 8,13. 
In cases, however, where the revision gocs deeper we 
need hardly assume mere arbitrary changes’ which their 
author made in accordance with his better knowledge, or 
because he thonght he knew better, but may rather ascribe 
these to strict adherence to a Pahlavi Avesta 
codex now lost.? La, Kr represent the tradition in 
Seistan, Jpr, Mfa the old written transmission of Yazd. 
Both transmissions, however, are still quite close to cach 
other. If it were our task to reconstruct the text of the

would appear from a critical standpoint a very hazardous

More extensive in material and at the same time more 
complicated is the manuscript transmission of the Yasna, 
Like the Vendidad, the Yasna has been handed down in 
a twofold form: first, the text combined with the old 
commentary; second, the sada-text with the ritual pre- 
scriptions (Nirang or Kiri), As to contents both forms 
of text are exactly alike. The external difference is even 
«less than in the Vendidad, except so far as the Mss. with 
the translation give the numerous repetitions by no means 
rarely in extenso, and on the other hand the sdda-text 
is by no means sparing of abridgment. Along with the 
Pahlavi translation we have also, for the greater part of 
the Yasna, the later Sanskrit translation by Neryosangh 
The latter, however, is based throughout on the Pahlavi 
translation; the Sanskrit Yasna Mas., therefore, form only 
a special group under the first class of manuscripts. The 
sada-texts, however, fall into two scparate classes, for 
in this case the regular Yasna sadas stand over against 
the Yasna of the Vendidad sadas. 

Only one manuscript of the Yasna with the Pahlavi 
translation was accessible to Westergaard, namely, the 
old Copenhagen Yasna, Ks, which he rightly regarded as 
his best codex. In details, however, he stond in need 
of a correct standard for testing the trustworthiness 
of the manuscript. Such a standard is afforded in the 
first place by the Pahlavi Yasna J2 which is only a few 
months older. According to the characteristic handwrit- 
ing and the colophons, both Mss. are by the well-known 
copyist Mitré-apan, the scribe of both old Pahlavi 
Vendidads. In Ks the copyist even mentions his source, 
the Ms. of his great-great-uncle Ristakhm, scribe of 
both the Vispereds in Copenhagen and of the original 
source of Kz, Lg, who must have prepared the manuscript 
about 1270,' In Ja, on the ether hand, Mitré-apan, con- 
trary to his custom elsewhere, is utterly silent as to his

Tt follows as a necessary consequence of this, that the 
continuer of Neryosangh’s Sanskrit translation must have 
used Kg. In fact he made Kg the basis of his continua- 
tion of 48-53, and with the help of this Ms. he revised 
at the same timc the text already translated. Now since 
Mitré-<ipan, however, wrote his Yasna in 1323, the con- 
tinuer of Neryosangh cannot possibly have been his cousin 
Onmazdyér, for Ormazdyar, the son of Ramyar, lived eight 
generations before Péshydtan who, in the year 1397, wrote

the colophon of the Munich manuscript of the Gésht-i

of @ generation at twenty five years, the result brings us 
to the end of the twelfth century as the date of Ormazdyar. 
‘This must also be about the date of Neryosangh. 

A further question now arises: which manuscript of the 
Pahlavi Yasna can Neryosangh have used for his work, 
and bad the Pahlavi Yasna already in his time split up

‘The Ms. in which the two lines converge as they 
tun back, cannot therefore be placed before Neryosangh, 
but it must be placed before 1280, at which time the 
Ms, of Rastam and probably also of his nephew Mitrd- 
Apan-f Spend-dad were written. Between the Ms. of the 
last named Mitré-Apan and that of Iarnbag, there inter- 
venes only a single Ms., that of Mah-panah-t Azdd- 
mard. This, affer all, must be the ancestral manuscript of 
both families of the Pahlavi Yasna and at the same time 
a sister manuscript of Neryosangh’s original source. Re- 
garding Rstam, we know from the second colophon in 
Kx, that he came from Iran to the land of the Hindus and 
there copied the Pahlavi Vendidid. Iie likewise copied 
the Vispered in 1278, in India, The Gosht-i Fryand,* 
however, he probably copied in Iran. Now, did he copy 
the Yasna in Iran or in India? If he copied it in India 
this cannot have been done directly from the Ms. of Mah- 
panah, for the latter's Ms. remained behind in Iran where it 
‘was transcribed nearly contemporaneoualy with Rastam, by 
Mitré-Apan-t Spend-dad. Rastam in that case must have 
brought with him to India another copy of the Mah-pandh 
Ms, a Ms. X from which the Indian Pahlavt Yasna is

descended. If he copied it in Iran, then the Ms. written 
by him must itself be the ancestral manuscript of the 
Indian line. ‘The former supposition that he copied the 
Yasna in India receives material support from Ja. Of 
the two nearly related Indian Yasna Mss., Jz and Ks, only 
one, namely, Kg, is positively a copy of the Rastam manu- 
script. As to Ja, however, it may in a measure be made 
probable that this Ms. is copied from an older Ms., thus 
from the original source of the Ristam Ms., which still 
existed in India in the year 1323. This would be the X 
assumed above, 

According to what has been said, all the Mss. of the 
Pahlavi Yasna, as far back as the Mah-panah Ms. inclusive, 
are later than Neryosangh (ca. 1200), As in all proba- 
bility he could derive his originals only from Iran, there 
comes into consideration, so far as he is concerned, only 
the Fambag Ms. (ca, 1110), The Farnbag Ms. itself, 
however, he cannot have used, for this remained in Tran 
where it was copied by Mah-panaéh ahout the time of 
Neryosangh. He must have had before him another 
copy (¥) of the Farnbag Ms., consequently a sister copy 
of the Mah-panah manuscript. The mutual relation of our 
manuscripts is fully in harmony with this supposition. 

The last question is this: how did Fambag come to 
combine his Pahlavi Yasna from two different Mss. instcad 
of being content with a single original? Probably be- 
cause in his time an Avesta-Pahlavi Yasna was no longer 
surviving, or rather had not yet come into existence. 
The ritual of the Yasna, as shown by positive evidence, 
goes back as far as Sassanian times; the Yasna texts 
themselves, however, with the Pahlavi translation, were 
inherent in the various Nasks, especially in the Stéd-Yasht 
Nask. The compilation of the text book Yasna may 
have been first undertaken even at a very late period. 
Might not the two 1)asturs Mah-yar and Mah-vindad (about 
1020) have first separately undertaken this work and 
Farnbag have united their newly edited texts for the 
first time into Avesta-Pahlavi Yasna?' In that case the 
Introduction in Ptq would disclose the cntire history

‘The Paris Ms. No. 14 of Dastur Shapir, who was 
xtill known to Anquetil (i,1 p. 460), evidenUy bears the 
marks of the text revision which has been popular with 
the copyists since the time of Jamasp and arab, 

Up to this point I have silently assumed that the old 
Copenhagen Ms, 7a is the Ms, of Rastam, the great- 
great-uncle of Mitr-Apin. It must not, however, be passed 
over in silence that Westergaard (Pref. p. 13) expressed 
doubt as to the authenticity of the Ms., and that even 
to-day his doubt does not appear to be wholly unjustifi- 
able, ct us briefly present again the facts in the case, 
‘The old portion of the Ms. K7 begins with the Vispered 
sida (K7b); to this a Nirang and an Avesta fragment are 
appended as closing prayers; then follows on fol. 107 the 
colophon with the name of the copyist, namely, Rida- 
stakhm (Rastam), son of Mitré-apan, and the date 627 
of the Persian era (A.D, 1288, or more probably 1273). 
Then follows on fol. 108 by the same hand the Pahlavi 
Vispered without any special postscript. The position 
of the colophon is striking, One may conceive that 
Ristam at first copied only the sada-text and finished it, 
and that later a Pahlavi Ms. of the Vispered came into 
his hands, and that he added a copy of this to the former. 
In this event the colophon of K7b would count also for 


PROLEGOMENA. 


Kya, at least so far us the copyist is concerned; not, 
however, of course with reference to the exact date. The 
Ms. accordingly would be sixty-five (or forty-five) years 
older than the four well-known Mas, of Mitrd-apan of 
1323 and 1324; yct in spite of this, the Ms. has come 
to us in far better condition than the other four. This 
may have been Westergaard’s special ground of objection. 
It is chiefly the bad ink, however, that has worked de- 
structively in the case of Mitré-dpan; as an actual fact 
the paper of Kza-b could be so old. If Westergaard 
be in the right, then the Ristam Ms. existed only in a 
younger copy and the copyist transcribed the colophon 
of the original without adding his own postscript. In 
this case the colophon would count of course only for 
the sida-text and there would not be the slightest ground 
of proof to the effect, that the Pahlavi Vispered also goes 
back to a Ristam manuscript. 

The question as to genuineness arises also in the case 
of the old composite codex Kao whose style of writing 
in many respects recalls Vispered K7. The Ms. Kao has 
@ series of colophons for the various texts, and among 
them are three with names and dates. In all three the 
well-known Mitré-dpan is mentioned as copyist. The first, 
on fol. 38a after the Gosht-i Fryand, is dated on the day 
Rashn of the month Din of the year 690 A. Y. (-: November 8, 
1321); the second, after the Hadhékht-Nask, on the day 
Rashn of the month Atir of the Parst year 720+ 20 
after Yezdegerd (= August 28,1371); the third, after the 
Shdyast-la-shiyast, on the day Adar of the month Mihr 
of the Parsi year 700 (= July 30, 1331). Consequently 
an unnatural order 1321, 1371, 1331. The middle date 
is particularly striking on this account, that in such case 
Mitré-4pan would have done the copying full fifty years 
after his carliest work of the year 1321, whereas West 
reckons the sixtieth year of age as the extreme limit of 
activity of a copyist. The date must therefore rest upon 
a mistake in writing. Moreover, the long interval between 
the first and second colophon is in contradiction to the 
entire Ms. which appcars to be written in a single style, 
and that not the characteristic handwriting of Mitré-apan. 
In this case therefore Westergaard (Pref. p. 3 n.1) was un- 
questionably right in believing that Kae was not written 
by Mitré-apan himself, but it is certainly a very old copy 
of a scribe who copied in onc composite codex a serics 





of smaller Mes. and among these certainly three of Mitré- 
pan and transferred the colophons of his originals with- 
out making additions. 

Kao has a series of texts in common with M6. The 
Ms. M6, likewise a collective codex, comes from the copyist 
Péshydtan and is dated A.Y, 766 (A.D. 1397). West 
has treated of the relation of these two in S.B./:. vol.v, 
Inter. 30. Both Mss. are nearly related and are either 
copied from the same original, and Kao in fact some 
years earlicr than M6; or Kao is transcribed from an 
older copy of the original of M6; but in no case is M6 
copied from K20. lor some texts Péshyétan certainly 
used a Ristam manuscript. His postscript to the Arda- 
Viraf and Gésht-i Fryano (ef. Haug and West, The Hook 
of Arda Viraf p. 266) bears witness to this, Now since 
the Pahlavi Vispered in M6 is a direct and very cxact copy 
of K7a, the fact just mentioned would again speak in 
favor of the genuinencys of the Rastam manuscript. But 
as no second Raistam Ms. has been preserved which would 
render possible a comparison of the handwriting, the 
question remains unsolved, The fuct that Kza is the 
Pahlavi Vispered which is to be taken as a basis, remains 
established, for the converse relation -K7a a copy of M6 
—is excluded: M6 has several slight inferioritics in the 
text as opposed to K7a, but never an older, better reading: 
than the latter. The Ms, Kya must under any circum- 
stances therefore be placed before 1397.

All the texts that remain of the Avesta proper, after 
excluding the trio Yasna-Vispered-Vendidad, are com- 
prised for the most part under the collective name Khorda 
Avesta, although the application of the term in so extended. 
a sense is not justified. These texts contain a twofold 





element: the Yashts and the minor prayer formulas. 
The latter make up the chief contenta of the Khorda 
of small Avesté in the proper sense of the term, which 
is a book designed for the use of the laity. A sharp 
line of distinction, however, no longer exists. Certain 
Yashts which were already contained in the Bakin-Yasht- 
Nask, the real Yasht book of the Sassanian Avesta,’ form 
an integral part of most Khorda Avestis. Conversely, 
the Yasht codexes are preceded by the same pieces 
{alphabet, prayers, Nydishes) as the lay-breviarics. It is 
only for the texts of the Khorda Avesta that we can 
assume a continuous oral transmission and a consequent 
development of a “Vulgate”; whereas the great Yashis 
have been preserved almost exclusively by written trans- 
mission. The texts of the great Yashts are far less 
common, but inasmuch as the scribe has not been con 
stantly infinenced by a memorized text, they have been 
far more accurately handed down from transcript to tran- 
script. 

If we first divide the respective Mys. according to 
their contents, we shall have three groups: 

(1) the pure Yasht Mss., the chief representative of which 
is Fr, the old Ms. of Asadin; 

(2) the Khorda Avestds in the strict sensc of the term 
{one of the most comprehensive Mas. is 03); 

(3) the combined Mss., a combination of No. 1 and 2 
into a great collective volume (a type of this group 
is Ptr). 

Only No. 1 and No. 3 call for detailed description. In 
order to make clear the relation of the first group to the 
third I shail begin with the sixteenth or Din-Yasht. At 
first glance the text of this Yasht appears to be split up 
into two recensions. In reality, however, the one recen- 
sion is mercly the very corrupt Vulgate of the samc text 
which is fairly correctly transmitted in other manuscripts. 
This corrupt Vulgate may be traced as far back as the 
fourteenth century. It is to be found already in Jong 
(A. 1). 1352), although the corruption had not yet so far 
advanced. The corrupt Vulgate text is the text of the 
Khorda Avest4 transmission, but the better text is that 
of the Yasht transmission. Fr, Ex, K16 share in the latter,

Although in the case of the Yasht Mss. and the com- 
bined Mas., the general relations are clearly established, 
it is no longer possible to bring any order into the mass 
of the Khorda Avestas proper. These have been pro- 
duced apparently in India as in Persia in considerable 
numbers during the last two centuries. ‘They vary much in 
compass. IJardly two Mas, are to be found which agree 
exactly in contents and arrangement. Their componition 
dcpended upon the pleasure of the copyists, who probably 
for the most part availed themselves of material from 
various sources. So much only can be said, that both of 
the Khorda Avestas with Neryosangh's Sanskrit translation, 
Jo and Ha, and the two with Bhisha translation, Lg and 
Mba, stand very close together. With few exceptions those 
pieces of text that really contain the least matter were the 
ones that were most in favour with the Khorda Avesta 
copyists. In spite of the mass of manuscripts the restora- 
tion of the text has been but little furthered by these; 
a low estimate may be put upon the critical value of most 
of the manuscripts, An exception which lends a ray of 
sunshinc amid the dreary work of collating and examining 
the Khorda Avestd Mas., is made by the Mss. of Jranian 
extraction. These stand in the same relation to the Indian 
ones as the Vendidad sidas of the two countries stand 
to each other; and beside being better prepared than the 
Indian manuscripts, they also presuppose a more solid 
written and oral tradition. For those Yashts, therefore, 
which are selected by preference for the Khorda Avestas, 
we have a threefold transmission: (1) the Yasht trans- 
mission proper in India, represented by ¥2; (2) the Per- 
sian source; (3) the Vulgate of the Indian Khorda Avestas. 
These three transmissions stand in an analogous relation 
to each other to that in which the three sources of the 
Vendtdad stand. The Yasht transmission proper answers 
in this case to the Pahlavi Vendidad in the latter. As 
the Pahlavi Vendidad is more nearly related to the Pere 


aly 


sian Vendidad sada, so Fs in many respects stands nearer

source, It occupies an intermediate position between Fx 
and the Persian manuscripts. Of primary importance 
among the Persian manuscripts of the Khorda Avesta arc 
Fa, Mfg, Kg6, K38; of secondary importance arc Ki8a, 
E37, W1, W3, Pd, Kha, Las, Lbs, Lbx6.”

Yt. 3.

signated as such. Sometimes, however, it is difficult to

been as far as possible to free the text from these em- 
barrassing additions, and in this endeavour I had the 
support principally of the Persian manuscripts which are 
almost free from glosses. 

The higher criticism has therefore only a slight field 
of activity in the Avesta. The attempt to distinguish 
between what is old and what is new in the remnants 
Preserved in the final Sassanian redaction of the Avesta 
canon, is a hopeless undertaking. An edition of the text 
must be kept free from any such attempt. Its sole effort 
must be to arrive at the stage of the ultimate and final 
redaction of the text, which took place, in part at least, 
a considerable time after the last Yezdegerd. In many 
cases, even this will remain an unattainable ideal, for we 
are obliged to rest content with what the manuscripts 
authenticate. 

So much the more is there opportunity, however, for 
the lower text criticism in the Avesta. The form of single 
words fluctuates in the Mss., sometimes more, sometimes 
less. The method which I followed in reconstructing the 
test, or to speak frankly, the method which I acquired, like

There are, especially, two influences at work which 
tend to detract from the fidelity of the manuscripts. On 
the one hand, the copyists knew the majority of their 
texts by heart. The oral text, however, had become 
more corrupted than the written text and keeps con- 
atantly crossing the latter. Scribes who read and copied

The number 72, however, is traditional for the Yasna. 
The Yasna Mss. sometimes do not agree in regard to 
the close of chapters, or do not mark the end distinctly. 
It is 10 be observed that the introduction to a new 
chapter is frequently drawn over into the close of the 
preceding chapter. In my edition the Vispered has one 
more chapter than in Westergaard. I have divided Wester- 
gaard’s Karde 23 into two, in accordance with the Vendi- 
dad sida. The division of the great Yashta into Kardes 
is carefully carried out in the good manuscripts. The 
division into paragraphs is based everywhere upon Wester- 
gaard, 

Punctuation is a weak point in the manuscripts. 
They have various signs of punctuation, indeed, but 
they have no system of punctuation. I had to devise a 
system for myself, based upon the signs that are found: 
thus, + is a colon, + semicolon or period, *7 denotes the 
close of a paragraph or the end of a sentence, ¢ a greater 
division, ¢y¢: the end of a chapter. In texts with Pahlavi 
and Sanskrit translation, this version takes the place of 
punctuation The text is cut up by the translation into 
sentences of varied length, sometimes of only one or two 
words, Kor the most part, however, the explanation is 
inserted at an actual break in the sentence. It is only 
in the rarest instances that the manuscripts vary in this 
traditional division of the sentence.’ In the sida-texts, 
on the contrary, the text runs along without break until 
the first large division, with a mark of punctuation thrown 
in only here and there.? A general exception is made 
in the Gathas, where the close of the strophe is regularly 
denoted by the star. Where the translation was wanting 
T was therefore often thrown upon my own resources as 
regards punctuation. In that case the punctuation may 
be regarded in doubtful instances simply as subjective. 
In the Vendidad I have adhered almost absolutely to the 
division of sentences by the Pahlavi translation, and have 
indicated the samc cither by a larger point (.), or by x 
where the sentence ends, I regret that J did not do this 





consistently also in the Yasna; although even there the 
larger point for the most part denotes a division by the 
translation.*

The variant readings have been aclected in such a

The metre which is plainly transparent in many texta, 
I have brought out clearly to the eye in print, although 
the diaskeuasts had no longer any idea of this metre.” 
These verses, however, are not perfect, whether this be 
due to the mediocre character of the metrical skill of 
the composers, or to the fact that the texts have passed 
through a re-editing. The sign is placed before such 
imperfect verses. The symbol * is used to mark words 
that are suspicious. For the reasons above discussed, 
however, I have grown more and more cautious and 
Sparing in the use of these signs as the work went on. 
The symbol * is employed for a sign of abbreviation and 
repetition, exactly as it is in the manuscripts. In the 
notes, much more extensive use has becn made of * for 
the sake of cconomizing space.

Finally, the imposing list of names of men and in-

names of the magnanimous Dasturs in Bombay. Dastur

open freely to me the treasures of his manuscripts. He 
not only contributed the most largely from those in his 
own possession, but he also induced many of his fellow- 
countrymen to do the same. It was cspecially due to 
his incessant urging that the important manuscripts Fr, 
Jp3, 8: were intrusted to me by their owners. In the 
second place I have the pleasure of mentioning Dastur 
FPeshotanji Behramji Sanjana, His four manuscripts 
accompanied the work from the beginning to the end, 
Among Dastur Hoshangji Jamaspji's manuscripts, I 
should have been especially unwilling to miss the old 
Yasna,

Khurshedji Rustamji Cama Esqr., very obligingly sought 
out the most important among them for my use. Of the 
European Libraries, the India Office in London and 
the University Library in Copenhagen stand in Avesti- 
cis at the head. R. Rost, that ever ready promotor 
of Oriental science, placed the entire manuscript material 
at my disposal from the first preliminary work on the 
edition almost to the completion of the printing. Only 
those who have had experience in such matters and know 
how important the personal examination of the manu-

due to the Administration of the Royal Library in Munich. 
Also the Bodleian Library, in spite of inconvenience 
at the time, arranged to send its three manuscripts to 
Tubingen. For the exception made in my favour I have 
to thank the request of the Curator, F. Max Miller, 
made in my behalf. The University Library of Bombay 
sent three manuscripts upon the spontancous application 
of G. Buhler. The Cambridge codex was loaned to me 
after the late Professor William Wright in most generous 
manner had stood surety for me. 

T desire to express my respectful thanks to the German 
Foreign Office which, upon intercession from high 
authority, arranged for the transportation of the manu- 
scripts, and provided the Imperial Consul in Bombay 
with special instructions to this end. In like manner 
T desire to thank the Ministry of Public Instruction 
in Prussia and in Wurtemberg, which allowed the 
manuscripts to be deposited and used in the libraries 
under their charge. 

This edition, indeed, would not have been possible

thanks to Reinhold Rost through whose kind help such

“Westergaard has created for himself a pecu- 
-Mar aystem of punctuation, since that of the Manu- 
scripts, especially those without translation, is 
altogether insafficient. { have extended his system, 
‘sGiding several new marks the form of which are 
borrowed from the Manuscripts, Thus » repre- 
sents our colon ‘and semicolon, * our full-stop, 
v a larger break, vv the end of a chapter. 
1 have retained Westergaard’s larger stop as the 
smallest, punctuation. In many places 1 have cm- 
ployed the larger stop. for the sole reason that 
the Manuscripts with translation maite a break at 
that point. It was impossible to follow slavishly 
the punctuation of the Manuscripts, which indeed 
do not agtee among themseives, since they often 
split up matter which is closely connected. Where 
however the division into clauses “in the Pahlavi
